snippet.title: The Fall of Holland: The (Staggering) Siege of Haarlem 1572/73 | Eighty Years' War
snippet.description:
Stay informed, not influenced. Upgrade the way you consume news by subscribing to Ground News — the platform that helps you see every side of the story. Get 40% off the Vantage Plan for unlimited access by using my exclusive link: https://groundnews.com/sandrhoman This is a limited-time offer, so don’t miss out.

On December 18, 1572, a Spanish army under Don Fadrique Álvarez de Toledo opened fire on the Dutch city of Haarlem. This marked the beginning of a siege characterized by extensive mine warfare, a naval battle on the Haarlemmermeer, and the valiant efforts of armed citizens—including the famous Kenau Simonsdochter Hasselaer. The stakes were high—Haarlem had thrown its lot in with the Dutch Revolt, determined to free itself from the grip of Spanish rule. Don Fadrique wanted to nip this uprising in the bud by wiping out Haarlem and its rebellious inhabitants. This is how modern historiography tells the story of the staggering siege of Haarlem.

snippet.title: Battle of the Triple Walls - Third Punic War (Part 2) DOCUMENTARY
snippet.description:
The Siege of Carthage kicks off with a mass assault by land and sea! 🐢TMNT have arrived in RAID! Join Leonardo, Donatello, Raphael, Michelangelo, April & Shredder in the ultimate crossover event💥 
Download RAID iOS/Android/PC ➡️ https://t2m.io/Invicta_Oct25 today to get exclusive heroes 🎉 Available after downloading through this link only
✅1 - Epic Tagoar from the start
✅2 - Epic Fayne after reaching level 15
⌛Kick off your collection with 6 TMNT Champions — just log in for 7 days before October 30

In part 1 of this series we covered the opening stage of the Third Punic War. This involved a recap of the inter-war years where Carthage focused on internal recovery while Rome continued its external expansions. However as Carthage slowly recovered, this prompted Rome to clamp down on them to prevent the potential for any future threat the African power might pose. What followed was a lopsided strongarming of the Carthaginians to force them into ever more humiliating terms of peace. Finally, enough was enough and the Punic city stood up.

In this episode we cover the ensuing Siege of Carthage as the legions descend on Africa to take the city by force. Yet while they thought it would be a simple affair, what followed would be a brutal siege that dragged on for nearly 4 years. This would begin with a combined land and sea assault against the triple walls of Carthage.

Stay tuned as we prepare to cover the siege of Carthage in full detail.

snippet.title: One Helmet Feature That Won Battles for Rome #military #history
snippet.description:
Roman centurions (31 BC-AD 500) wore their helmet crests sideways, not front-to-back like legionaries. This wasn't decoration—it was tactical design. In battle chaos, soldiers needed to identify their centurion from any angle to follow commands and rally. A longitudinal crest (front-to-back) was only visible from the front or rear. A transverse crest (side-to-side) was visible from all directions. Centurions also wore bronze greaves (shin guards) while legionaries fought with bare legs—this was an instant visual status marker. They carried the vitis, a vine staff used both as a symbol of rank and a disciplinary tool to beat soldiers. One centurion, nicknamed "Cedo Alteram" (Gimme Another), broke so many vine staffs beating his men that he was the first centurion killed during the Pannonian Mutiny in 14 AD. Centurions made 15 times what legionaries earned and led from the front rank, resulting in twice the casualty rate. Trajan's Column in Rome (113 AD) shows centurions with transverse crests, greaves, and vine staffs—you can still see it today. This is the Imperial Roman centurion, reconstructed from archaeological evidence.

#RomanCenturion #AncientRome #ImperialRome #TrajansColumn #WarriorReconstruction #RomanArmy #MilitaryHistory

In July 1216, Prince Louis of France set up his siege artillery before the walls of Dover Castle. The French  prince had come to England to support a group of rebel barons against King John of England, occupying much of the country and now aiming to capture Dover Castle, known as “the key to England.” The castle controlled the shortest sea route to France and thus Louis’s connection to his logistical base at home. The siege of Dover Castle was characterized by the use of new types of artillery, brutal assaults, and near-impenetrable defenses. The very future of England hung in the balance: what began as a dispute over the barons’ rights, enshrined in the famous Magna Carta, quickly escalated into a full-scale French invasion—and Dover Castle stood as one of the last strongholds of resistance. This is how modern historiography tells the story of the staggering siege of Dover Castle.

snippet.title: How Leif Erikson Found North America — And Why Nobody Stayed
snippet.description:
In 1021 AD, a Norse axe cut down a tree in Newfoundland, Canada. We know the exact year because of the tree ring. It is the earliest confirmed date of European presence in North America — 471 years before Christopher Columbus arrived in the Caribbean.
The expedition was led by Leif Erikson, son of Erik the Red. He had heard accounts from a sailor named Bjarni Herjulfson, who had sighted unknown land to the west of Greenland years earlier and kept sailing without going ashore. Leif bought Bjarni's ship and retraced his route in reverse with a crew of thirty-five men.
Three landfalls. The first — Helluland, Land of Flat Stone — was glaciers and bare rock. The second — Markland, Woodland — was forested coast with white sand beaches. The third was different: salmon-filled rivers, wild grapevines, frost-free winters. A crew member named Tyrker found the grapes. Leif named it Vinland. They built houses and stayed the winter.
In 1960, Norwegian archaeologist Helge Ingstad and his wife Anne Stine Ingstad discovered the settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of Newfoundland. Carbon dating and tree-ring analysis confirmed the date: 1021 AD.
Bjarni saw a continent and kept sailing. Leif built a house on it.
📖 Further reading on Norse exploration: https://amzn.to/4tNEHCL
#LeifErikson #Vikings #NorthAmerica #Vinland #Shorts #HistoryShorts #TimelineHistory

snippet.title: The Conquistadors Harrowing & Doomed Quest For a Lost Civilization in the Amazon History Documentary
snippet.description:
In this history documentary I examine one of the most incredible and strangest expeditions in the history of exploration, as in 1541 Francisco De Orellana and his small force of Spanish conquistadors began a hopeful expedition into the heart of the Amazon jungle along the mighty Amazon river that snakes through it. 
What would follow were months of suffering, despair and doom as there quest to discover the lost city of gold - El Dorado - became a living nightmare, as not only their dreams were swallowed up by the infinite rainforest, but there very sanity. 
What survives is an incredible, but highly disputed account of wonders and phenomena that defy belief. 
Was their journey real? Or was it all just a lie created by desperate, failed men?

snippet.title: When Elephants Faced Rome — The Battle of Zama (202 BC)
snippet.description:
October 19, 202 BC. On a dusty plain in North Africa, the fate of the Western world hangs in the balance. 🌍💥 For sixteen years, Hannibal Barca—the man who had haunted Rome's nightmares since Cannae—stands with his back against the wall. No reinforcements. No hope of retreat. Just his veterans, his war elephants, and his genius against a Roman army led by a man who learned war by watching him. This is Zama: the battle where Rome finally faced its greatest enemy—and won. 🛡️🔥

In this video, we march onto that fateful field to witness the clash that ended the Second Punic War and sealed Rome's destiny as the master of the Mediterranean. Discover how Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus—the only Roman general who ever outthought Hannibal—turned Carthage's greatest weapons against them and destroyed an empire in a single afternoon.

snippet.title: "He Survived 17 DAYS Trapped in 'The Boats' - Ancient Persia's Most Brutal Punishment"
snippet.description:
In Ancient Persia, they had a punishment so horrifying that historians still debate whether it actually happened. They called it "The Boats" or Scaphism - and one man allegedly survived 17 days.

🔴 What You'll Discover:
- How the ancient Persian execution method "The Boats" actually worked
- The disturbing process: force-feeding, honey torture, and insect infestation
- The story of Mithridates - the soldier who survived 17 days in 400 BC
- Why historians question if this punishment was real or propaganda
- The historical evidence (or lack thereof) behind this brutal method
- How Greek writers may have exaggerated Persian cruelty

⚠️ CONTENT WARNING: This video discusses historical torture and execution methods. While no graphic imagery is shown, the descriptions are historically accurate and may be disturbing to some viewers.

📚 HISTORICAL CONTEXT:
Scaphism (from Greek "skaphe" meaning boat/tub) was allegedly an ancient Persian execution method used around 500-400 BCE for serious crimes like treason. The most famous documented case is Mithridates, a Persian soldier who allegedly survived 17 days after bragging about killing a prince.

However, the only historical sources are Greek writers like Plutarch, who wrote centuries after the alleged events and had strong anti-Persian biases. No Persian records, archaeological evidence, or physical artifacts have ever been found to confirm this practice existed.

🎓 EDUCATIONAL PURPOSE:
This video examines the historical claims, sources, and debates surrounding scaphism. It explores how ancient propaganda may have created exaggerated stories of enemy cruelty - a practice relevant to understanding historical bias and misinformation.

🔍 SOURCES & RESEARCH:
- Plutarch's "Life of Artaxerxes" (primary source)
- Ancient Greek historical accounts
- Modern historical analysis and scholarly debate
- Archaeological evidence examination (absence of proof)
- Comparative analysis with confirmed ancient punishments

📖 RELATED TOPICS COVERED:
- Ancient Persian justice system and laws
- Achaemenid Empire criminal punishment methods
- Greek-Persian Wars propaganda and bias
- Historical source reliability and verification
- Ancient execution methods across civilizations
- Archaeological evidence in historical claims

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS:
Understanding how historical accounts can be distorted by political bias helps us critically evaluate sources - a skill essential for understanding both ancient and modern information warfare.

snippet.title: Vlad Dracula's REAL Horror vs The Myths
snippet.description:
In 1462, an army of 90,000 soldiers marched into Wallachia to destroy one man.

They never fought him.

They turned back and fled.

This is the true historical account of Vlad III Dracula — Vlad the Impaler, the medieval ruler whose psychological warfare broke one of the largest armies of the age.

Chroniclers described a sight so horrifying that even Sultan Mehmed II, the conqueror of Constantinople, refused to advance.

This wasn’t myth.
This wasn’t legend.
This was real history.

⚔️ Watch till the end to understand why terror worked better than armies.

📌 Follow for more real medieval history, dark war stories, and untold legends.

#HistoryShorts #WarPsychology

snippet.title: How Did France Lose Control of Canada?
snippet.description:
The Battle of the Plains of Abraham in 1759 was one of the most daring attacks in history, a risky gamble that ultimately paid off for Britain and resulted in France losing control of Canada and most of her North American possessions. 
General James Wolfe led a small British army on a risky nighttime amphibious assault that took the French by surprise and resulted in the capture of Quebec and fall of Canada.

snippet.title: How Cats Conquered Ancient Egypt & Other Weird Ways Animals Won Battles in History
snippet.description:
In this history documentary I take a look at the Battle of Pelusium, a clash between the ancient empires of Persia and Egypt that saw cats deployed on the battlefield with stunning results. 
Did the presence of cats really win the battle for the Persians? I also take a look at some other weird and unusual ways animals and insects have been used in history to gain an advantage in battle. 
#documentary #history

snippet.title: Total War: Medieval 3 - Unit Roster Reveal (Holy Roman Empire)
snippet.description:
Unit rosters have been revealed for Total War: Medieval 3. The latest live stream and blog post go over the design philosophy behind unit rosters in the game. This involves 4 main categories of troop types:  Cultural group, Faction bloc, culture, and faction. We go over the nuances of this design philosophy and the reveal of the Holy Roman Empire faction.

snippet.title: How a Real Amazon Actually Looked, 2,500 Years Ago
snippet.description:
The Greeks called them Amazons and assumed they were a story. They were wrong. About one in three Scythian women was buried with weapons — and with the same war injuries, the same gold, and the same honors as the men beside them. When one of the largest armies of the ancient world marched into the steppe in 513 BC, the women who fought stayed behind to face it as equals.
This is what one of those warrior women really looked like.
📖 This episode was built from Osprey Publishing's The Scythians 700–300 BC — the source for the armor, the weapons, and the burial finds. Grab it here: https://amzn.to/4w2tRKL
Timeline History reconstructs the warriors history actually produced — their gear, their tactics, and the moments that defined them.
Whose face should we reconstruct next? Tell me in the comments.
